note.text: Phonetic symbols represent sounds, not ordinary letter names. The pair contrasts a voiceless model with a voiced model. Voicing concerns vocal-fold vibration, not capitals or loudness. Both are dental fricatives: the tongue approaches the teeth and air passes with friction. The screen supplies written models only. Use a teacher or reliable recording to practise the actual sounds; printed choices cannot assess your pronunciation.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to group written model words by their initial consonant and explain the stated voicing distinction. Builds on: written sound-symbol preparation and careful dictionary use. Leads to: clearer word recognition and later teacher-led pronunciation practice.

sections.heading: Understand the pattern
sections.text: Phonetic symbols represent sounds, not ordinary letter names. The pair contrasts a voiceless model with a voiced model. Voicing concerns vocal-fold vibration, not capitals or loudness. Both are dental fricatives: the tongue approaches the teeth and air passes with friction. The screen supplies written models only. Use a teacher or reliable recording to practise the actual sounds; printed choices cannot assess your pronunciation.

sections.heading: Read the original model
sections.text: Written model groups: think, thin, thank, thing begin with /θ/; this, that, these, those begin with /ð/. Compare the initial consonant, not the word’s final letter. Different spellings can sometimes represent the same sound, so spelling alone is not a universal pronunciation rule. These are standard model examples to verify with the teacher’s pronunciation convention.

sections.heading: Apply and check
sections.text: Identify which sound the model supplies, then group the written examples. For the actual contrast, listen to a model and practise separately with a teacher. Do not interpret a correct multiple-choice answer as proof that you have heard or produced the sound accurately. Word-initial examples avoid claiming that every occurrence of a letter combination behaves identically.
